summary: Defines requirements for EAP methods used in IEEE 802.11 wireless LANs, which use 802.1X and EAP under the IEEE 802.11i security amendment. The material was approved by IEEE.

eli5.summary: Wifi logins use a menu of checking methods. This memo says what a method must be able to do to be allowed on wifi.

questions: what are the eap method requirements for wireless lans
why is eap md5 not allowed for wifi
what is the eap msk and emsk
subtitle: The checklist an EAP method must pass before it is fit for IEEE 802.11 wireless LANs.

tldr.problem: IEEE 802.11i relies on IEEE 802.1X and the Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP), but many EAP methods exist and not all are strong enough to protect a wireless LAN.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC lists mandatory, recommended and optional features an EAP method must have, such as key derivation, 128-bit effective key strength and mutual authentication.
tldr.outcome: Methods that miss any MUST requirement, including EAP-MD5-Challenge, One-Time Password and Generic Token Card, are not compliant for wireless LAN use.

today: RFC 4017 is an Informational RFC and the metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated. It builds on RFC 3748.

sections.title: Why Wireless LANs Need Method Rules
sections.content:
The IEEE 802.11i security amendment makes use of IEEE 802.1X, which in turn relies on the Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP), defined in RFC 3748. Wireless LAN deployments of the time already used several EAP methods, including EAP-TLS, EAP-TTLS, PEAP and EAP-SIM, with credentials such as digital certificates, passwords, secure tokens and SIM secrets.

This document sets requirements for EAP methods used in IEEE 802.11 deployments. Its material was approved by IEEE 802.11 and is published for information. A method that claims conformance must complete IETF last call review.
sections.eli5: Wifi lets you prove who you are in many ways, like a password or a special card. This memo says which ways are safe enough.

sections.title: Terms and Compliance Levels
sections.content:
The authenticator is the end of the link that starts EAP authentication. The peer (called the supplicant in IEEE 802.1X) answers it. A backend authentication server may run the EAP method for the authenticator, and the EAP server is whichever entity ends the method with the peer.

Two keys matter. The Master Session Key (MSK) is keying material exported by the method and is at least 64 octets long. The Extended Master Session Key (EMSK) is also at least 64 octets, is not shared with the authenticator or any third party, and is reserved for future uses.

A method that fails any MUST or MUST NOT is not compliant. One that meets all MUST, MUST NOT, SHOULD and SHOULD NOT items is unconditionally compliant. One that meets only the MUST and MUST NOT items is conditionally compliant.
sections.eli5: Think of a test with must-pass questions and bonus questions. Pass only the must-pass ones and you are okay. Pass the bonus ones too and you get full marks.

sections.title: Mandatory Requirements
sections.content:
Credentials may be certificates, user names and passwords, existing secure tokens, or mobile network (GSM and UMTS) secrets. Whatever the credential, a method suitable for wireless LANs MUST meet seven criteria.

  • It generates symmetric keying material (the RFC 3748 "Key derivation" claim).
  • It can generate keying material with 128 bits of effective key strength, and exports an MSK and an EMSK of at least 64 octets each.
  • It supports mutual authentication.
  • Peer and server hold equivalent shared state when the method completes, and each learns the other's authenticated name.
  • It resists dictionary attacks.
  • It protects against man-in-the-middle attacks, covering cryptographic binding, integrity protection, replay protection and session independence.
  • If it negotiates a ciphersuite, that negotiation is protected.
sections.eli5: A good wifi login must make a fresh secret key, check both sides are who they say, and not be easy for a sneaky person to fool or guess their way past.

sections.title: Recommended and Optional Features
sections.content:
Methods SHOULD support fragmentation, because RFC 3748 says methods can assume a minimum EAP MTU of 1020 octets and SHOULD fragment payloads larger than that. They SHOULD also support end-user identity hiding, the confidentiality claim.

Methods MAY support channel binding and fast reconnect. Neither is needed to be compliant.
sections.eli5: Hiding who you are and quickly reconnecting are nice extras. They are good to have but not required.

sections.title: Methods That Fail the Test
sections.content: EAP-MD5-Challenge, described in RFC 3748 as the current mandatory-to-implement method, is non-compliant. So are One-Time Password and Generic Token Card. As RFC 3748 notes, none of them support any of the mandatory requirements, including key derivation and mutual authentication, nor any of the recommended or optional features.
sections.eli5: Some old login methods are like a lock with no key you can reuse and no way to check the door is real. They are not allowed on wifi.

sections.title: Mapping Requirements to Threats
sections.content:
Wireless networks give an attacker within range easy access, so EAP use in 802.11i faces the threats listed in RFC 3748. The RFC takes a list of required system properties from a presentation by Housley and shows which requirement answers each one.

  • Algorithm independence and ciphersuite negotiation: requirement 7.
  • Strong, fresh session keys: requirement 2.
  • Replay protection and the domino effect: requirement 6.
  • Authentication: mutual authentication (requirement 3), with identity protection as the recommended extra.
  • Key binding: the optional channel binding feature.

Authorization is left to other means, such as AAA protocols like RADIUS.
sections.eli5: Each rule on the list is there to stop a particular trick, like copying an old message or breaking into one door to get into the whole building.

items.label: Key strength
items.desc: MUST give 128-bit effective strength; MSK and EMSK of at least 64 octets.

items.label: Shared state
items.desc: MUST be equivalent on both sides at success.
